title: Prediction Accuracy at Key Stage 4
author: Katie Beynon and Dave Thomson
summary: Katie Beynon and Dave Thomson of FFT Education Datalab analyse around one million predicted-versus-actual GCSE grade pairs across 740 schools and 140,000 pupils, drawn from FFT's Aspire research project, to answer a narrower and more careful question than 'how accurately can teachers predict attainment': to what extent do predicted grades actually match results. They find that average predicted and actual grades are close in almost every subject -- with predictions usually running slightly higher than results -- but that this aggregate closeness masks much weaker pupil-level accuracy: in most subjects, fewer than half of individual predictions exactly matched the grade a pupil went on to achieve. Maths and the art and design subjects were the strongest performers by both measures, while English literature stood out as a case where average predicted and actual grades were nearly identical yet pupil-level matching was among the lowest of any subject (34%), illustrating that cohort-level accuracy and individual-level accuracy are genuinely different things that can diverge sharply. The authors are careful to flag three caveats -- inconsistent school assessment policies, varying collection timing, and the inherent unreliability of exam marking itself -- that limit how far the findings can be pushed toward a definitive claim about teacher judgement.
points: The paper's central methodological move is separating cohort-level accuracy (average predicted grade vs. average actual grade) from pupil-level accuracy (does each individual's prediction match their result) -- these turn out to diverge substantially by subject.

The headline finding is stark: across all subjects, only in maths and the three art and design subjects did more than 50% of individual predictions exactly match results, meaning most subjects saw the majority of individual predictions differ from outcomes.

English literature is the paper's sharpest illustration of the cohort/pupil divergence -- near-zero difference in average grades, yet only 34% of individual predictions matched exactly, one of the lowest rates of any subject.

The authors explicitly resist overclaiming: three named caveats (inconsistent school assessment policies, inconsistent collection timing, and inherent unreliability in exam marking itself) mean they frame the question as 'to what extent do predicted grades match results' rather than a definitive verdict on teacher accuracy.

Computer science had the largest average grade gap (0.4 grades higher predicted than achieved), while four subjects -- maths, combined science, photography, and English literature -- showed essentially zero average difference, again showing why average-grade comparisons alone can be misleading.
quotes: In total, 740 of our participating schools submitted both predicted grades and results. Overall, our dataset contains around 1 million predicted-actual grade pairs for 140 thousand pupils.

For these reasons, we don’t claim to be able to definitively answer a question like “how accurately can teachers predict attainment?” Instead, we’ll explore the more limited question “to what extent do the predicted grades made by teachers match their pupils’ results?

Computer science was the subject with the biggest difference in average grade, with predictions 0.4 grades higher than results, on average. There were four subjects where the difference in average grade between predictions and results rounds to zero.
English literature, despite having almost no difference between average predicted grades and results has one of the lowest percentages of predictions matching results, 34%.
Maths and the three art and design subjects are the only ones where more than 50% of predictions matched results.

Overall, most subjects are quite similar to each other in terms of average predicted grades vs results, with almost all subjects seeing differences of a quarter of a grade or less. There is more variation between subjects, however, when looking at the percentage of predictions which matched results.
Together, this implies that, nationally at least, predicted grades tend to match results quite closely at the cohort-level, but not at the pupil-level.
